topics.title: A story told by a chair

learn.hook: What if the chair you're sitting on could talk? What stories would it tell about you?
points: 'The Chair' is a story that centres on an ordinary chair and the feelings and imagination around it.
When a non-living thing is given human feelings or actions, it is called personification ('the chair felt young again').
A story told by 'I' is in the first person. The narrator here is the chair itself.
The setting is where and when a story happens; the characters are the people, animals or things in it.
Readers can infer (work out) feelings from clues, even when the feeling is not named.

example.q: Read: I am an old wooden chair on Nani's verandah. For forty years I have held tired visitors, giggling grandchildren and one very fat cat. My legs creak now, and yesterday someone said, "Let's throw it away." But little Chintu painted my arms blue and said, "You're my throne!" I felt young again. How does the chair feel at the start and at the end?
steps: 'My legs creak now' and 'Let's throw it away' suggest the chair feels old and unwanted.
Chintu paints it and calls it his throne.
'I felt young again' shows it now feels happy and loved.
example.answer: At first it feels old and unwanted; at the end it feels young, happy and loved.

learn.reallife: Many families keep an old chair, almirah or trunk for years — each one 'remembers' family stories!

games.title: The chair's story
items: The chair is on Nani's verandah.
The chair is made of plastic.
It is an old wooden chair.
The story is told by the chair.
The narrator says 'I am an old wooden chair'.
Chintu wanted to throw the chair away.
Someone else said that; Chintu painted it and called it his throne.
The chair has held a fat cat.
It has held 'one very fat cat'.

games.title: Personification or not?
items: The old door groaned as it opened.
The wind whispered through the trees.
The wind blew the papers away.

quiz.q: Who is the narrator of the chair story?
quiz.explain: The story begins 'I am an old wooden chair', so the chair tells it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the narrator must be a person

quiz.q: Where is the chair kept?
quiz.explain: The first line tells us the setting: Nani's verandah.
quiz.mistake: Does not find the setting in the first line

quiz.q: In the story, "For forty years I have held tired visitors, giggling grandchildren and one very fat cat." What does this tell us?
options: The chair is very old and has been used a lot
The chair belongs to the cat
The chair was in a shop for forty years
quiz.explain: Forty years of holding many people shows the chair is old and well used.
quiz.mistake: Misses the meaning of 'forty years'

quiz.q: "My legs creak now." Here the chair's 'legs' are:
options: the wooden legs of the chair
quiz.explain: A chair has legs too — its wooden supports — and they creak because they are old.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'legs' to mean only human legs

quiz.q: Which line shows personification?
quiz.explain: A chair cannot really feel; giving it feelings is personification.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what personification means

quiz.q: Why did Chintu call the chair 'my throne'?
options: He loved it and imagined it as a king's seat
quiz.explain: Calling a painted old chair a throne shows love and imagination.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'throne' literally

quiz.q: The chair story is told in the:
quiz.explain: The narrator uses 'I', which is the first person.
quiz.mistake: Does not link 'I' with first-person narration

quiz.q: Which word best describes Chintu?
quiz.explain: He turned an old chair into a 'throne' in his mind and with paint.
quiz.mistake: Does not judge character from actions

teach.ask: Gappu is amazed: 'In this story the chair talks and feels! Is that allowed in English?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Giving human feelings to things is personification. Maybe my nest has feelings too!
teach.nudge: What do we call it when a non-living thing is given human feelings?

learn.hook: A blanket can be a tent, a broom can be a horse, and a chair can be a throne — all you need is imagination!
points: Imagination is the power to form pictures and ideas in your mind of things that are not really present.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when) and a plot (what happens, with a problem and an ending).
Writers often start with a 'What if...?' question: What if my school bag could fly?
Word family: imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginative (adjective), imaginary (adjective: not real).
'Imaginative' describes a creative person or idea; 'imaginary' describes something that exists only in the mind.

example.q: Think it through: Ananya writes: 'What if the old chair could walk at night?' Name the parts she needs to build a story.
steps: Character: the old chair (and maybe the family).
Plot: a problem (the chair wants to explore) and an ending (it returns before morning).
example.answer: She needs characters, a setting and a plot with a problem and an ending.

learn.reallife: Cardboard-box rockets, rangoli designs and the games you invent with friends all come from imagination.

items.text: Close your eyes and ___ you are on the Moon.
Riya is an ___ girl who writes lovely stories.

quiz.q: What is imagination?
options: The power to lift heavy things
The power to picture ideas in your mind that are not really present
quiz.explain: Imagination lets us picture things that are not in front of us.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of the word

quiz.q: Which word is the adjective meaning 'existing only in the mind, not real'?
quiz.explain: Something imaginary is not real; it exists only in the mind.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the noun and the adjective

quiz.q: Which sentence uses 'imaginative' correctly?
options: Ravi has an imaginative friend who is not real.
Ravi is an imaginative boy who invents new games.
quiz.explain: Imaginative means creative, so it describes Ravi well. An unreal friend would be 'imaginary'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses imaginative (creative) with imaginary (not real)

quiz.q: In a story, the 'setting' means:
options: where and when the story happens
quiz.explain: The setting is the place and time of the story.
quiz.mistake: Confuses setting with characters or moral

quiz.q: What is the 'plot' of a story?
options: the series of events that happen
quiz.explain: The plot is what happens in the story from start to end.
quiz.mistake: Confuses plot with setting

quiz.q: Which is the best 'What if...?' story starter?
options: I go to school by bus.
What if my school bag could fly me to school?
quiz.explain: It asks an imaginative question that can lead to a fun story.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a plain fact instead of an imaginative idea

quiz.q: Chintu imagines the old chair is a king's throne. This shows he is:
options: telling a lie to hurt someone
quiz.explain: Pretending a chair is a throne is creative, imaginative play.
quiz.mistake: Confuses pretend play with lying

quiz.q: What is the verb in the word family imagine, imagination, imaginative?
quiz.explain: 'Imagine' is the action word (verb); the others are a noun and an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Cannot tell parts of speech apart in a word family

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I want to write my own story about a flying chair. What do I need?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Imagination plus characters, a setting and a plot — my flying chair story is ready to take off!
teach.nudge: Besides imagination, what parts does every story need?

learn.hook: Empathy is like trying on someone else's shoes — even a chair's! — to feel what they feel.
points: Empathy means understanding and sharing the feelings of another person (or imagining how a thing or animal might feel).
Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy goes further — you imagine yourself in their place.
Feeling words help us show empathy: lonely, hurt, proud, grateful, nervous, relieved.
Conjunctions are joining words: and (adds), but (contrasts), or (gives a choice), so (shows result), because (gives a reason).
Example: 'The chair felt sad because someone wanted to throw it away, but Chintu loved it.'

example.q: Think it through: Join with the right conjunction: 'Meena's friend was crying. Meena sat beside her and listened.'
steps: The second sentence is the result of the first.
example.answer: Meena's friend was crying, so Meena sat beside her and listened.

learn.reallife: When a classmate loses a match or a pet, saying 'I can imagine how hard that is' shows empathy.

items.text: The chair was old, ___ Chintu still loved it.
Raju felt lonely ___ his best friend had moved away.
It started raining, ___ we went inside.
Tara painted the chair ___ put it in the sun to dry.

quiz.q: What is empathy?
options: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
quiz.explain: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else's place and feeling with them.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of empathy

quiz.q: Which sentence shows empathy?
options: "I know you're upset about losing; I felt the same last year."
quiz.explain: It shows understanding of the other person's feelings.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise caring words

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Arjun was very tired, ___ he still finished his homework.'
quiz.explain: 'But' shows a contrast: tired, yet he still finished.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'so' or 'because' where a contrast is needed

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Priya smiled ___ she won the drawing prize.'
quiz.explain: Winning was the reason she smiled; 'because' gives a reason.
quiz.mistake: Does not identify a reason in the sentence

quiz.q: Which word is a conjunction?
quiz.explain: 'Because' joins two parts of a sentence, so it is a conjunction.
quiz.mistake: Confuses joining words with other parts of speech

quiz.q: How is empathy different from sympathy?
options: Empathy means imagining yourself in the other's place and sharing the feeling
quiz.explain: Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy is feeling with them from their point of view.
quiz.mistake: Thinks empathy and sympathy are opposites

quiz.q: A new student sits alone at lunch. What shows empathy?
options: Invite her to sit with your group
quiz.explain: Imagining how lonely she feels and including her shows empathy.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the other person's feelings

quiz.q: Which conjunction gives a choice?
quiz.explain: 'Or' gives a choice between two things.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the jobs of different conjunctions

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Everyone says I should have empathy. What is it, and how can I show it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Empathy means feeling what someone else feels, as if I were in their place. I'll listen and help!
teach.nudge: How does empathy help you understand another person's feelings?
